Header:
Date: 2026-12-20

Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Devon Patel (Redwood Solutions), Priya Nair (Skyline CISO), Tom Reynolds (Skyline Head of Platform), Aisha Malik (Skyline Security Eng)

Summary (auto): Security review focused on encryption and key management. Customer emphasized HIPAA and data residency; looking for assurance around BYOK/HSM and auditability.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Carlos our SE - real quick, purpose of today is to run through our encryption posture and key management options, and answer any compliance questions.
[00:08] Priya Nair: Hi Maya, thanks. We're especially focused on HIPAA controls for PHI, encryption at rest/in transit, and how keys are managed. We prefer BYOK if possible and need details on HSM support.
[00:18] Carlos Ruiz: Absolutely. We'll cover hosted, dedicated, and private options and how we integrate with external KMSes and HSMs. Quick note, some of the product names maybe auto-corrected in notes - hope that's okay.
[00:25] Tom Reynolds: That's fine. Also care about audit logs retention and proof that keys can't be exported.
[00:30] Devon Patel: Great point. So at a high level, Redwood supports envelope encryption - service data keys (DEKs) are used to encrypt payloads and are then encrypted with a customer or Redwood master key (KEK). We can integrate with AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, and with Cloud HSM / external HSM providers for BYOK.
[00:45] Aisha Malik: When you say integrate, do requests flow to our KMS on every token generation, or do you cache wrapped keys locally? We need to know about latency and failover.
[00:53] Carlos Ruiz: Good question. In hosted mode, we use envelope encryption and call the customer-managed KMS for unwrap/wrap operations during key rotation and initial key provisioning. For performance we cache the encrypted DEKs and keep DEKs in memory in protected processes; unwrap isn't called on every request. We also support a fallback where Redwood-managed keys are used if the customer KMS is unavailable, but that is only with explicit agreement - chain-of-custody requirements usually rule that out for customers who insist on BYOK.
[01:15] Priya Nair: So for strict HIPAA we would want no fallback to Redwood keys. Is that supported?
[01:20] Carlos Ruiz: Yes. For Dedicated or Private deployments we can enforce no-fallback policies. In Private deployments, the control plane can be customer-managed and keys never leave your control.
[01:28] Tom Reynolds: How about HSM - we use an on-prem Thales nShield. Can Redwood talk to an on-prem HSM?
[01:34] Maya Chen: We do have patterns for hybrid HSMs. For hosted we can integrate with cloud HSMs (AWS CloudHSM, Google Cloud HSM) natively. For on-prem HSMs we typically route via a customer-side connector or proxy in their VPC that performs KMS operations and the Redwood service calls that proxy endpoint. That connector can be run as part of a Private deployment or in a VPC peering arrangement.
[01:54] Aisha Malik: That proxy - is it a black box we have to trust? What about authentication, mTLS?
[02:00] Carlos Ruiz: The connector uses mutual TLS and SAS policies. We authenticate with mTLS and OAuth tokens scoped to key operations. We log every call and include request IDs to match application logs. The connector can be audited and run inside your network.
[02:10] Priya Nair: And for Cloud HSM like AWS CloudHSM - does Redwood support hardware key storage where the keys never leave the HSM?
[02:16] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, with AWS CloudHSM and AWS KMS you can use a customer-managed key where the root material is in the HSM. Our integration supports using AWS KMS CMKs and CloudHSM-backed keys; Redwood never persists plaintext key material.
[02:26] Tom Reynolds: How are key rotations handled? We need automated rotations and a way to prove rotation happened for auditors.
[02:31] Devon Patel: Redwood supports scheduled rotations and on-demand rotations. For BYOK we orchestrate rotation via calls to your KMS and we keep an immutable rotation log - which is an append-only audit record that shows key version changes, timestamps, and the actor (service account or user). We can surface that in the Console or push to your SIEM via secure log forwarding.
[02:49] Aisha Malik: Are audit logs tamper-evident?
[02:52] Carlos Ruiz: We provide chained log entries and integrate with your log ingestion; customers can route logs to CloudWatch, Stackdriver, or send them to a customer-managed GCS/S3 bucket with retention controls. For higher assurance, Private deployments can integrate with your nonrepudiation store.
[03:04] Priya Nair: What about encryption in transit - TLS versions, ciphers?
[03:08] Maya Chen: We enforce TLS 1.2+ and recommend TLS 1.3 where supported. We rotate server certificates regularly and support customer-provided certs in Private deployments. Cipher suites are restricted to modern AEAD suites; we can provide the exact list in the security pack.
[03:21] Tom Reynolds: Data residency - our PHI must stay in US regions. Can we restrict region?
[03:25] Carlos Ruiz: Yes. We support region pinning and customer routing policies. For Hosted we have region control; Dedicated and Private give you full control over where data lands.
[03:33] Aisha Malik: Quick question on PKI and key zeroization. If we decommission a key, what's the guarantee you don't retain any plaintext or key material?
[03:41] Devon Patel: Redwood never persists plaintext DEKs to disk. For KEKs managed by customer KMS or HSM, only the KMS/HSM holds the plaintext root material. When a key is retired we zeroize cached in-memory DEKs and remove references; for Private deployments you can require a physical key destruction procedure. We can also provide a key destruction certificate if needed for audits.
[04:01] Priya Nair: Do you support per-tenant keys? We need logical separation between customers.
[04:06] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, each customer gets distinct KEKs and DEKs. For multi-tenant hosted customers we recommend customer-managed KEKs per account. For Dedicated/Private it's one-to-one by default.
[04:15] Tom Reynolds: About RBAC and SSO - how are key operations gated?
[04:20] Maya Chen: We have RBAC in the Console and role-based API scopes. We integrate with SSO providers via SAML/OIDC and support SCIM for provisioning. Key operations require separate privileges; separation of duties can be enforced via roles.
[04:32] Aisha Malik: And how long are encryption-related audit logs retained? Our policy is seven years for some records.
[04:36] Carlos Ruiz: Default retention is 90 days in the Console; enterprise plans and Dedicated/Private allow configurable retention and long-term archival to your buckets for compliance (S3/GS). We can support 7 years subject to storage and contract terms.
[04:49] Priya Nair: For the BYOK flow, can you walk through a typical onboarding sequence?
[04:53] Devon Patel: Sure. 1) Customer creates a master key in their KMS/HSM. 2) Provide an IAM/service account with limited permissions or deploy the connector in their network. 3) We exchange certificates and establish mTLS. 4) Redwood requests the wrapped key metadata and stores only the encrypted DEKs. 5) We run test decrypts during onboarding and provide audit evidence. After that, runtime uses envelope encryption with in-memory DEKs.
[05:16] Tom Reynolds: What about emergency key revocation or compromise procedure?
[05:19] Carlos Ruiz: We support immediate key disable via KMS calls. If a KEK is revoked, DEKs encrypted under that KEK become unrecoverable unless you have a backup key. We recommend a key-rotation and backup policy; we can help model RTO and recovery tradeoffs in the PoC.
[05:31] Aisha Malik: Any limitations for large models or long context windows? I know KV caches and tokenization can expose temporary data - how is that handled?
[05:38] Maya Chen: Our runtime keeps KV caches in memory on GPUs; we don't persist prompt material to disk unless you enable logging or transcript storage. For PHI we recommend disabling transcript storage and enabling strict logging to your SIEM. Also for Dedicated/Private, those caches never leave your VPC.
[05:53] Priya Nair: Can we get a signed attestation that Redwood follows SOC 2 controls around encryption?
[05:58] Maya Chen: Yes - we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 reports available under NDA. We'll send the artifacts.
[06:03] Tom Reynolds: Are there known gotchas with HashiCorp Vault integration?
[06:06] Carlos Ruiz: Vault works fine; we use Vault Transit for envelope workflows. The main gotcha is network connectivity and token TTLs - make sure the Vault tokens or AppRole TTLs align with Redwood's connector refresh policy. We'll include config examples.
[06:19] Aisha Malik: For HSM models, do you support FIPS validations?
[06:24] Devon Patel: Yes, Cloud HSMs and many on-prem HSMs are FIPS-capable; we can map device validation strings in the compliance pack.
[06:33] Priya Nair: One last question - key escrow. Do you provide any escrow for keys?
[06:38] Carlos Ruiz: We do not escrow customer KEKs by default. If you need a split-escrow or third-party escrow solution, that's something we can design as a contractual add-on with strict controls.
[06:48] Maya Chen: Okay, let's go through a quick recap and next steps.
[06:51] Maya Chen: Action items: we'll send the SOC 2/ISO docs, a KMS integration diagram, and a BYOK runbook; schedule a POC deep dive to test AWS CloudHSM integration and key rotation; customer to share compliance checklist and HSM vendor model. Any other items?
[07:06] Priya Nair: That covers it. Thanks.
[07:08] Tom Reynolds: Thanks everyone.
[07:10] Carlos Ruiz: We'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite.

[End of transcript]
